3. Evaluation Methodology

3.1 Design

The evaluation used a pre-post design without a control group. Baseline data were collected during the first two weeks of the programme in February 2024. Endline data were collected during the final three weeks of the programme in November 2024. This design allows us to track within-participant change but cannot attribute observed changes solely to the programme.

3.2 Data Sources

| Instrument | Administered | Respondents | Response Rate |
|------------|--------------|-------------|---------------|
| Participant pre-survey | Feb 2024 | 85 students | 100% |
| Participant post-survey | Nov 2024 | 82 students | 96.5% |
| Mentor feedback form | Mar, Jul, Nov 2024 | 40 mentors | 92.5% |
| Teacher baseline report | Feb 2024 | 62 teachers | 100% |
| Teacher endline report | Nov 2024 | 58 teachers | 93.5% |
| Attendance records | Ongoing | – | – |
| Focus groups | Jun 2024 | 24 students | – |

3.3 Measures

The participant survey included 18 items across four domains: academic confidence, future orientation, help-seeking behaviour, and relationship with mentor. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Teacher reports assessed classroom engagement, homework completion, and participation in class discussions using a 3-point scale.

3.4 Analysis

Descriptive statistics were computed for all variables. Paired t-tests were used to compare pre- and post-programme scores for participants with complete data (n = 82). Effect sizes are reported using Cohen's d. Focus group transcripts were analysed thematically.

4. Participant Profile

A total of 85 students were enrolled in LYMP for 2024. The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 reports that Lantern Youth Mentorship Programme participant_count_2024 is 85 students. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the final enrolment confirmation on 1 February 2024.

Table 1: Enrolment by Cohort and School Level

| CH-BP1 | Secondary 2 | 22 | 21 |
| CH-BP2 | Secondary 2–3 | 24 | 23 |
| CH-NS | Secondary 3–4 | 21 | 20 |
| CM-TP | Secondary 1–2 | 18 | 18 |
| Total | – | 85 | 82 |

Notes: CH = school-based cohort; CM = community-based cohort. One student in CH-BP1 withdrew in April; one in CH-BP2 withdrew in July; one in CH-NS withdrew in September. All withdrawals were due to family relocation.

5. Outcome Findings

5.1 Academic Confidence

Mean academic confidence scores increased from 2.9 (SD = 0.8) at baseline to 4.3 (SD = 0.6) at endline, a mean increase of 1.4 points (t(81) = 12.6, p < 0.001, d = 1.9). The proportion of students who agreed or strongly agreed with the statement "I believe I can succeed in my studies" rose from 41% to 88%.

5.2 Future Orientation

Scores on the future orientation domain increased from a mean of 3.1 (SD = 0.7) to 4.0 (SD = 0.6), representing a mean increase of 0.9 points (t(81) = 9.8, p < 0.001, d = 1.3). In focus groups, students frequently referenced the value of "seeing what is possible after O-Levels" and learning about polytechnic and ITE pathways from their mentors.

5.3 Help-Seeking Behaviour

Help-seeking scores increased from 2.7 (SD = 0.9) to 3.6 (SD = 0.8), a mean increase of 0.9 points (t(81) = 7.4, p < 0.001, d = 1.0). At endline, 76% of students reported they would approach a teacher or counsellor if they faced a problem at school, compared to 44% at baseline.
## 6. Programme Completion and Retention

### 6.1 Completion Rate

The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 reports that Lantern Youth Mentorship Programme completion_rate is 0.82 proportion. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the final programme close on 30 November 2024.

Completion is defined as a participant who (a) remained enrolled through the end of their cohort's programme cycle, (b) attended at least 70% of scheduled mentorship sessions, and (c) completed both the baseline and endline surveys. A participant who met the attendance threshold but did not complete the endline survey was classified as a completer for attendance purposes but excluded from outcome analyses; this affected one student in CH-NS.

Of the 85 students enrolled, 82 completed the programme, representing an overall completion rate of 96.5%. The 0.82 proportion referenced above reflects the completion rate as a proportion of the full enrolled cohort. Table 2 below presents completion by cohort and reason for non-completion.

**Table 2: Completion and Non-Completion by Cohort**

| Cohort | Enrolled | Completed | Completion Rate | Non-Completion Reason |
|--------|----------|-----------|-----------------|-----------------------|
| CH-BP1 | 22 | 21 | 95.5% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, April) |
| CH-BP2 | 24 | 23 | 95.8% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, July) |
| CH-NS | 21 | 20 | 95.2% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, September) |
| CM-TP | 18 | 18 | 100.0% | – |
| **Total** | **85** | **82** | **96.5%** | **3 withdrawals** |

### 6.2 Attendance

Session attendance was recorded by mentors using the programme's mobile check-in application and verified against physical sign-in sheets at each session. Where discrepancies existed between the two records, the physical sign-in sheet was treated as authoritative.

Mean session attendance across the programme was 91.2% (SD = 6.8%). Attendance was highest in the CM-TP cohort (94.6%) and lowest in CH-NS (88.9%). The lower attendance in CH-NS is attributed to the timing of sessions, which were held on Wednesday afternoons during the school term; several students in this cohort cited CCA commitments as a scheduling conflict. In response, two sessions in Term 3 were rescheduled to Saturday mornings, after which attendance in this cohort improved by approximately 7 percentage points.

### 6.3 Withdrawal Analysis

All three withdrawals were attributed to family relocation, as confirmed through exit interviews with the respective families. None of the withdrawals were related to programme dissatisfaction or mentor-student mismatch. The timing of withdrawals—April, July, and September—corresponded with the end of school terms, which is consistent with relocation patterns tied to housing transitions.

In each withdrawal case, the programme team conducted a brief exit conversation with the student and their guardian, and offered a referral to the school's counselling team where appropriate. One family accepted the referral. No withdrawn students were replaced mid-cycle, as the programme design did not permit late enrolment after the second session.

### 6.4 Retention Support

Retention support was provided through three mechanisms:

1. **Mentor check-ins**: Mentors were required to flag any student with two consecutive unexcused absences to the programme coordinator within 48 hours. This occurred in 12 instances across the year; in each case, the coordinator contacted the family and the student returned to regular attendance.
Out of scope for this evaluation were: long-term academic attainment (e.g., PSLE or O-Level results), which will be assessed in a future longitudinal follow-up; and outcomes for family members or caregivers, which were not systematically measured in this cycle.

#### 7.2 Data Collection Timeline

Data collection followed a structured timeline across the year, with each instrument administered at predetermined points. Table 7.1 summarises the schedule; the sections that follow describe each instrument in more detail.

**Table 7.1: Data collection schedule**

| Instrument | Baseline | Midline | Endline | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Student SDQ (self-report) | 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-26 | 2024-07-08 to 2024-07-19 | 2024-11-18 to 2024-11-29 | — |
| Teacher SDQ (proxy report) | 2024-01-22 to 2024-02-02 | 2024-07-15 to 2024-07-26 | 2024-11-25 to 2024-12-06 | — |
| Academic engagement survey | 2024-01-29 to 2024-02-09 | 2024-07-22 to 2024-08-02 | 2024-12-02 to 2024-12-13 | — |
| Mentor session logs | — | — | — | Continuous |

The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 covers the evaluation_period from 2024-01-01 to 2024-12-31. Record status: current.

Baseline data collection was scheduled to occur after the Chinese New Year school break but before the programme's second session, to avoid the disruption of the holiday period. This timing was agreed with the partner schools in November 2023. Midline data collection was scheduled for the first two weeks of the school holidays in June/July, which allowed for data collection without disrupting classroom time. Endline data collection was scheduled for late November and early December, before the final programme sessions concluded on 2024-12-14.

All surveys were administered in paper form during school hours, with a member of the M&E team present to read items aloud where needed. Surveys were available in English and Chinese; no students requested the Chinese version during this cycle.

#### 7.3 Instruments and Measures

**Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ).** The SDQ is a 25-item behavioural screening questionnaire. The student self-report version was used for students aged 11 and above; the teacher proxy version was used for all students. The SDQ produces scores across five subscales (emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour) and a total difficulties score. For this evaluation, we report the total difficulties score and the prosocial behaviour subscale. The SDQ was scored using the standard 0–2 Likert scoring, with the total difficulties score ranging from 0 to 40. Higher scores on the total difficulties scale indicate greater difficulties; higher scores on the prosocial subscale indicate greater strengths.

**Academic engagement survey.** This is an internally developed 12-item instrument measuring attitudes toward school, perceived relevance of schoolwork, and classroom participation. Items are scored on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = strongly agree). The instrument was piloted with 15 students in November 2023 and refined for item clarity. The internal consistency of the scale in the baseline administration was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha = 0.78).

**Mentor session logs.** Mentors completed a structured log after each session, recording the session date, duration, activities covered, and any concerns about the student's wellbeing or engagement. Logs were submitted through a secure mobile form within 48 hours of the session. These logs provided the primary source data for the attendance and retention analyses in Sections 6.2 and 6.4.
## 8. Challenges and Lessons Learned

This section draws on the quarterly programme reviews, mentor debrief sessions, and the end-of-year stakeholder workshop held on 2024-12-10. Challenges are grouped by theme; each is accompanied by the evidence base for the finding and the action taken or recommended.

### 8.1 Challenge: Sustained Mentor Availability

Mentor turnover was higher than projected. Of the 42 mentors who completed training in January 2024, 11 (26%) did not complete the full programme year. Seven resigned between March and June, citing work commitments or relocation; four paused participation in the third quarter and did not return. The planned mentor-to-student ratio of 1:3 was maintained for most students, but two schools experienced periods where the ratio fell to 1:5 for three to four consecutive weeks.

Evidence: Mentor session logs for the affected schools show a dip in session coverage during May and again in late September. In one school, 12 of 18 scheduled sessions in May were delivered; the shortfall was covered in June through double sessions, which mentors reported as tiring.

Recommendation: Introduce a structured co-mentor model for the 2025 cycle, pairing each lead mentor with a trained backup who can step in within one week. Revise the mentor commitment form to include a minimum notice period and a clear offboarding process.

### 8.2 Challenge: Student Engagement in the Final Quarter

Attendance at mentor sessions declined in the final quarter of the school year. Average monthly attendance was 87% from March to August, then fell to 79% in September, 74% in October, and 71% in November. The dip was most pronounced among Secondary 3 students preparing for end-of-year examinations.

Evidence: Attendance records show that 61% of missed sessions in the final quarter were attributed to examination preparation or extra classes. Mentor logs for this period frequently note that students asked to end sessions early to return to revision, with several mentors flagging that the session content felt less relevant during the exam season.

Recommendation: Adjust the programme calendar in 2025 so that the core mentoring curriculum concludes by early October, with a lighter "exam support" module offered in November. This module would focus on study skills and stress management rather than the standard curriculum.

### 8.3 Challenge: Data Collection Gaps

Despite the presence of an M&E officer at each survey administration, complete data were not obtained for all participants. The baseline survey was completed by 97% of enrolled students (n = 211 of 218); the endline survey was completed by 89% (n = 194 of 218). The primary reasons for missing endline data were student withdrawal from the programme (n = 12) and absence on the survey day (n = 12).

Evidence: Comparison of baseline and endline responders shows that students missing the endline survey had, on average, lower baseline attendance (62% vs. 84%) and higher baseline SDQ total difficulties scores (mean 17.4 vs. 14.9). This suggests that the students lost to follow-up may have been among those with greater difficulties, and their absence from the endline sample should be considered when interpreting the programme effects reported in Section 6.

Recommendation: For the 2025 cycle, schedule a make-up survey window of one week after the primary administration. Consider collecting a short exit form for students who withdraw, capturing reason for withdrawal and a brief wellbeing check.
### 8.4 Challenge: Survey Instrument Length and Clarity

The baseline and endline surveys, while adapted from validated instruments, were noted by several students as being long and containing items that were difficult to interpret. The baseline survey took an average of 22 minutes to complete (range: 14–38 minutes), exceeding the 15-minute target. The endline survey took an average of 18 minutes.

Evidence: Field notes from the survey administrations record that 14 students asked for clarification on the SDQ items, particularly the reverse-scored items. Two students commented that the question on "household chores" in the demographic section was confusing because they were unsure whether to include time spent helping at a family business. A small number of students (n = 6) left the open-ended feedback question blank, writing "nothing" or "not sure" in the space provided.

Recommendation: For 2025, shorten the demographic section by removing the household chores item and combining two questions on living arrangements. Pilot the revised survey with a small group of students (n = 8–10) in January 2025 to check comprehension and timing. Consider providing a brief verbal introduction to the SDQ before administration.

### 8.5 Challenge: Mentor Consistency and Quality

Mentor retention was generally strong, with 84% of mentors (n = 47 of 56) completing the full programme year. However, a small number of mentoring pairs experienced disruptions due to mentor unavailability during the mid-year school holidays and the December festive period.

Evidence: Mentor attendance records show that 9 mentors missed more than two consecutive sessions during the programme year. Of these, 5 were university students who had final examinations in May and November, and 2 were working professionals who travelled for business during the June holidays. In 4 of these cases, the mentee had a period of three or more weeks without a mentoring session.

Recommendation: Build a small pool of trained relief mentors (n = 5–6) who can step in for a maximum of two consecutive sessions. This pool should be recruited and trained by March 2025, with a brief orientation in April. Mentors should also be encouraged to communicate planned absences at least two weeks in advance, and the programme coordinator will track this in the mentor log.

---

## 9. Data Quality and Methods

### 9.1 Data Sources

The findings in this report draw on the following data sources, all collected between January and December 2024:

- **Pre-programme survey (baseline):** Administered in the first two weeks of January 2024, before the first mentoring session. Completed by 211 of 218 enrolled students (97%).
- **Post-programme survey (endline):** Administered in the last two weeks of November 2024. Completed by 194 of 218 enrolled students (89%).
- **Attendance records:** Recorded by mentors after each session and verified monthly by the programme coordinator. Covers all 36 scheduled sessions per student.
- **Mentor logs:** Submitted by mentors after each session, providing qualitative notes on session content, student engagement, and any concerns.
- **Focus group discussions:** Held in March (n = 12 students) and October (n = 10 students), facilitated by the M&E Officer with a note-taker present.
- **Mentor exit interviews:** Conducted with 12 mentors who left the programme or indicated they would not return in 2025.

documents.content:
3. Evaluation Methodology

3.1 Design

The evaluation used a pre-post design without a control group. Baseline data were collected during the first two weeks of the programme in February 2024. Endline data were collected during the final three weeks of the programme in November 2024. This design allows us to track within-participant change but cannot attribute observed changes solely to the programme.

3.2 Data Sources

| Instrument | Administered | Respondents | Response Rate |
|------------|--------------|-------------|---------------|
| Participant pre-survey | Feb 2024 | 85 students | 100% |
| Participant post-survey | Nov 2024 | 82 students | 96.5% |
| Mentor feedback form | Mar, Jul, Nov 2024 | 40 mentors | 92.5% |
| Teacher baseline report | Feb 2024 | 62 teachers | 100% |
| Teacher endline report | Nov 2024 | 58 teachers | 93.5% |
| Attendance records | Ongoing | – | – |
| Focus groups | Jun 2024 | 24 students | – |

3.3 Measures

The participant survey included 18 items across four domains: academic confidence, future orientation, help-seeking behaviour, and relationship with mentor. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Teacher reports assessed classroom engagement, homework completion, and participation in class discussions using a 3-point scale.

3.4 Analysis

Descriptive statistics were computed for all variables. Paired t-tests were used to compare pre- and post-programme scores for participants with complete data (n = 82). Effect sizes are reported using Cohen's d. Focus group transcripts were analysed thematically.

4. Participant Profile

A total of 85 students were enrolled in LYMP for 2024. The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 reports that Lantern Youth Mentorship Programme participant_count_2024 is 85 students. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the final enrolment confirmation on 1 February 2024.

Table 1: Enrolment by Cohort and School Level

| Cohort | School Level | Students Enrolled | Students Completed |
|--------|--------------|-------------------|--------------------|
| CH-BP1 | Secondary 2 | 22 | 21 |
| CH-BP2 | Secondary 2–3 | 24 | 23 |
| CH-NS | Secondary 3–4 | 21 | 20 |
| CM-TP | Secondary 1–2 | 18 | 18 |
| Total | – | 85 | 82 |

Notes: CH = school-based cohort; CM = community-based cohort. One student in CH-BP1 withdrew in April; one in CH-BP2 withdrew in July; one in CH-NS withdrew in September. All withdrawals were due to family relocation.

5. Outcome Findings

5.1 Academic Confidence

Mean academic confidence scores increased from 2.9 (SD = 0.8) at baseline to 4.3 (SD = 0.6) at endline, a mean increase of 1.4 points (t(81) = 12.6, p < 0.001, d = 1.9). The proportion of students who agreed or strongly agreed with the statement "I believe I can succeed in my studies" rose from 41% to 88%.

5.2 Future Orientation

Scores on the future orientation domain increased from a mean of 3.1 (SD = 0.7) to 4.0 (SD = 0.6), representing a mean increase of 0.9 points (t(81) = 9.8, p < 0.001, d = 1.3). In focus groups, students frequently referenced the value of "seeing what is possible after O-Levels" and learning about polytechnic and ITE pathways from their mentors.

5.3 Help-Seeking Behaviour

Help-seeking scores increased from 2.7 (SD = 0.9) to 3.6 (SD = 0.8), a mean increase of 0.9 points (t(81) = 7.4, p < 0.001, d = 1.0). At endline, 76% of students reported they would approach a teacher or counsellor if they faced a problem at school, compared to 44% at baseline.

## 6. Programme Completion and Retention

### 6.1 Completion Rate

The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 reports that Lantern Youth Mentorship Programme completion_rate is 0.82 proportion. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the final programme close on 30 November 2024.

Completion is defined as a participant who (a) remained enrolled through the end of their cohort's programme cycle, (b) attended at least 70% of scheduled mentorship sessions, and (c) completed both the baseline and endline surveys. A participant who met the attendance threshold but did not complete the endline survey was classified as a completer for attendance purposes but excluded from outcome analyses; this affected one student in CH-NS.

Of the 85 students enrolled, 82 completed the programme, representing an overall completion rate of 96.5%. The 0.82 proportion referenced above reflects the completion rate as a proportion of the full enrolled cohort. Table 2 below presents completion by cohort and reason for non-completion.

**Table 2: Completion and Non-Completion by Cohort**

| Cohort | Enrolled | Completed | Completion Rate | Non-Completion Reason |
|--------|----------|-----------|-----------------|-----------------------|
| CH-BP1 | 22 | 21 | 95.5% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, April) |
| CH-BP2 | 24 | 23 | 95.8% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, July) |
| CH-NS | 21 | 20 | 95.2% | 1 withdrawal (family relocation, September) |
| CM-TP | 18 | 18 | 100.0% | – |
| **Total** | **85** | **82** | **96.5%** | **3 withdrawals** |

### 6.2 Attendance

Session attendance was recorded by mentors using the programme's mobile check-in application and verified against physical sign-in sheets at each session. Where discrepancies existed between the two records, the physical sign-in sheet was treated as authoritative.

Mean session attendance across the programme was 91.2% (SD = 6.8%). Attendance was highest in the CM-TP cohort (94.6%) and lowest in CH-NS (88.9%). The lower attendance in CH-NS is attributed to the timing of sessions, which were held on Wednesday afternoons during the school term; several students in this cohort cited CCA commitments as a scheduling conflict. In response, two sessions in Term 3 were rescheduled to Saturday mornings, after which attendance in this cohort improved by approximately 7 percentage points.

### 6.3 Withdrawal Analysis

All three withdrawals were attributed to family relocation, as confirmed through exit interviews with the respective families. None of the withdrawals were related to programme dissatisfaction or mentor-student mismatch. The timing of withdrawals—April, July, and September—corresponded with the end of school terms, which is consistent with relocation patterns tied to housing transitions.

In each withdrawal case, the programme team conducted a brief exit conversation with the student and their guardian, and offered a referral to the school's counselling team where appropriate. One family accepted the referral. No withdrawn students were replaced mid-cycle, as the programme design did not permit late enrolment after the second session.

### 6.4 Retention Support

Retention support was provided through three mechanisms:

1. **Mentor check-ins**: Mentors were required to flag any student with two consecutive unexcused absences to the programme coordinator within 48 hours. This occurred in 12 instances across the year; in each case, the coordinator contacted the family and the student returned to regular attendance.

#### 7.2 Data Collection Timeline

Data collection followed a structured timeline across the year, with each instrument administered at predetermined points. Table 7.1 summarises the schedule; the sections that follow describe each instrument in more detail.

**Table 7.1: Data collection schedule**

| Teacher SDQ (proxy report) | 2024-01-22 to 2024-02-02 | 2024-07-15 to 2024-07-26 | 2024-11-25 to 2024-12-06 | — |
| Academic engagement survey | 2024-01-29 to 2024-02-09 | 2024-07-22 to 2024-08-02 | 2024-12-02 to 2024-12-13 | — |

The Lantern Impact Evaluation 2024 covers the evaluation_period from 2024-01-01 to 2024-12-31. Record status: current.

Baseline data collection was scheduled to occur after the Chinese New Year school break but before the programme's second session, to avoid the disruption of the holiday period. This timing was agreed with the partner schools in November 2023. Midline data collection was scheduled for the first two weeks of the school holidays in June/July, which allowed for data collection without disrupting classroom time. Endline data collection was scheduled for late November and early December, before the final programme sessions concluded on 2024-12-14.

All surveys were administered in paper form during school hours, with a member of the M&E team present to read items aloud where needed. Surveys were available in English and Chinese; no students requested the Chinese version during this cycle.

#### 7.3 Instruments and Measures

**Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ).** The SDQ is a 25-item behavioural screening questionnaire. The student self-report version was used for students aged 11 and above; the teacher proxy version was used for all students. The SDQ produces scores across five subscales (emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour) and a total difficulties score. For this evaluation, we report the total difficulties score and the prosocial behaviour subscale. The SDQ was scored using the standard 0–2 Likert scoring, with the total difficulties score ranging from 0 to 40. Higher scores on the total difficulties scale indicate greater difficulties; higher scores on the prosocial subscale indicate greater strengths.

**Academic engagement survey.** This is an internally developed 12-item instrument measuring attitudes toward school, perceived relevance of schoolwork, and classroom participation. Items are scored on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = strongly agree). The instrument was piloted with 15 students in November 2023 and refined for item clarity. The internal consistency of the scale in the baseline administration was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha = 0.78).

**Mentor session logs.** Mentors completed a structured log after each session, recording the session date, duration, activities covered, and any concerns about the student's wellbeing or engagement. Logs were submitted through a secure mobile form within 48 hours of the session. These logs provided the primary source data for the attendance and retention analyses in Sections 6.2 and 6.4.

documents.content:
## 8. Challenges and Lessons Learned

This section draws on the quarterly programme reviews, mentor debrief sessions, and the end-of-year stakeholder workshop held on 2024-12-10. Challenges are grouped by theme; each is accompanied by the evidence base for the finding and the action taken or recommended.

### 8.1 Challenge: Sustained Mentor Availability

Mentor turnover was higher than projected. Of the 42 mentors who completed training in January 2024, 11 (26%) did not complete the full programme year. Seven resigned between March and June, citing work commitments or relocation; four paused participation in the third quarter and did not return. The planned mentor-to-student ratio of 1:3 was maintained for most students, but two schools experienced periods where the ratio fell to 1:5 for three to four consecutive weeks.

Evidence: Mentor session logs for the affected schools show a dip in session coverage during May and again in late September. In one school, 12 of 18 scheduled sessions in May were delivered; the shortfall was covered in June through double sessions, which mentors reported as tiring.

Recommendation: Introduce a structured co-mentor model for the 2025 cycle, pairing each lead mentor with a trained backup who can step in within one week. Revise the mentor commitment form to include a minimum notice period and a clear offboarding process.

### 8.2 Challenge: Student Engagement in the Final Quarter

Attendance at mentor sessions declined in the final quarter of the school year. Average monthly attendance was 87% from March to August, then fell to 79% in September, 74% in October, and 71% in November. The dip was most pronounced among Secondary 3 students preparing for end-of-year examinations.

Evidence: Attendance records show that 61% of missed sessions in the final quarter were attributed to examination preparation or extra classes. Mentor logs for this period frequently note that students asked to end sessions early to return to revision, with several mentors flagging that the session content felt less relevant during the exam season.

Recommendation: Adjust the programme calendar in 2025 so that the core mentoring curriculum concludes by early October, with a lighter "exam support" module offered in November. This module would focus on study skills and stress management rather than the standard curriculum.

### 8.3 Challenge: Data Collection Gaps

Despite the presence of an M&E officer at each survey administration, complete data were not obtained for all participants. The baseline survey was completed by 97% of enrolled students (n = 211 of 218); the endline survey was completed by 89% (n = 194 of 218). The primary reasons for missing endline data were student withdrawal from the programme (n = 12) and absence on the survey day (n = 12).

Evidence: Comparison of baseline and endline responders shows that students missing the endline survey had, on average, lower baseline attendance (62% vs. 84%) and higher baseline SDQ total difficulties scores (mean 17.4 vs. 14.9). This suggests that the students lost to follow-up may have been among those with greater difficulties, and their absence from the endline sample should be considered when interpreting the programme effects reported in Section 6.

Recommendation: For the 2025 cycle, schedule a make-up survey window of one week after the primary administration. Consider collecting a short exit form for students who withdraw, capturing reason for withdrawal and a brief wellbeing check.

documents.title: Impact Evaluation Report 2024
documents.content:
### 8.4 Challenge: Survey Instrument Length and Clarity

The baseline and endline surveys, while adapted from validated instruments, were noted by several students as being long and containing items that were difficult to interpret. The baseline survey took an average of 22 minutes to complete (range: 14–38 minutes), exceeding the 15-minute target. The endline survey took an average of 18 minutes.

Evidence: Field notes from the survey administrations record that 14 students asked for clarification on the SDQ items, particularly the reverse-scored items. Two students commented that the question on "household chores" in the demographic section was confusing because they were unsure whether to include time spent helping at a family business. A small number of students (n = 6) left the open-ended feedback question blank, writing "nothing" or "not sure" in the space provided.

Recommendation: For 2025, shorten the demographic section by removing the household chores item and combining two questions on living arrangements. Pilot the revised survey with a small group of students (n = 8–10) in January 2025 to check comprehension and timing. Consider providing a brief verbal introduction to the SDQ before administration.

### 8.5 Challenge: Mentor Consistency and Quality

Mentor retention was generally strong, with 84% of mentors (n = 47 of 56) completing the full programme year. However, a small number of mentoring pairs experienced disruptions due to mentor unavailability during the mid-year school holidays and the December festive period.

Evidence: Mentor attendance records show that 9 mentors missed more than two consecutive sessions during the programme year. Of these, 5 were university students who had final examinations in May and November, and 2 were working professionals who travelled for business during the June holidays. In 4 of these cases, the mentee had a period of three or more weeks without a mentoring session.

Recommendation: Build a small pool of trained relief mentors (n = 5–6) who can step in for a maximum of two consecutive sessions. This pool should be recruited and trained by March 2025, with a brief orientation in April. Mentors should also be encouraged to communicate planned absences at least two weeks in advance, and the programme coordinator will track this in the mentor log.

---

## 9. Data Quality and Methods

### 9.1 Data Sources

The findings in this report draw on the following data sources, all collected between January and December 2024:

- **Pre-programme survey (baseline):** Administered in the first two weeks of January 2024, before the first mentoring session. Completed by 211 of 218 enrolled students (97%).
- **Post-programme survey (endline):** Administered in the last two weeks of November 2024. Completed by 194 of 218 enrolled students (89%).
- **Attendance records:** Recorded by mentors after each session and verified monthly by the programme coordinator. Covers all 36 scheduled sessions per student.
- **Mentor logs:** Submitted by mentors after each session, providing qualitative notes on session content, student engagement, and any concerns.
- **Focus group discussions:** Held in March (n = 12 students) and October (n = 10 students), facilitated by the M&E Officer with a note-taker present.
- **Mentor exit interviews:** Conducted with 12 mentors who left the programme or indicated they would not return in 2025.
